Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

protest noun

a public demonstration

also demonstration, protest march, demonstrator, protester, protesters, rally, take to the streets

classical

Cic. Verr. 2.4.52: quem concursum in oppidō factum putātis?
M-O s.v. demonstration: populī concursus

concursus, concursūs m.

often with populī; to hold one, concursum facere, declension

a crowd gathering; a demonstration

A running together of people, and so an uproar, a tumult (Lewis & Short); Morgan–Owens gives populī concursus for a public protest, and Egger concursum facere for demonstrating. It also means a clash, a collision.

Other words

  • sēcessiō plēbis — the plebs’ walk-out: Rome’s mass protest

    also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 1.62 (Lewis & Short); Liv. 2.32 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. demonstration

    The people of Rome left the city in a body until their demands were met; sēcessiō alone is a withdrawal, a secession (Lewis & Short).

  • prōtestātiō, prōtestātiōnis f. — a demonstration

    noun, third declension · also used · modern · Traupman 302

    Traupman’s word; in late Latin a declaration (Symmachus, the Vulgate; Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • quem concursum in oppidō factum putātis, quem clāmōrem, quem porrō flētum mulierum?

    what a gathering of people do you think there was in the town, what shouting, and what weeping of women besides?Cic. Verr. 2.4.52

See also protest, government.

SourcesLewis & Short: concursus · Lewis & Short: secessio · Lewis & Short: protestatio

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. demonstration, public protest.
